1:
Why this piece of furniture is described here rather than with the rest of the holy place is a question Ellicott raises and declines to answer. He sees no reason to suspect the text has been disturbed — the way Aaron is spoken of a few verses on presupposes his consecration, and incense had already been named among the offerings God would require. Clarke notes that the Samaritan Pentateuch does move the first ten verses, placing them earlier in the account.

What incense was doing in worship at all Ellicott answers from outside Israel. Its preciousness, its fragrance, and its seeming to mount in cloud after cloud to heaven gave it a natural place in worship, and many nations had found the same use for it: Egyptian priests appear on the monuments with censers, the inscriptions recording that it came from Arabia; Herodotus reports a thousand talents' weight of it consumed yearly at the feast of Belus; the Greek and Roman use is well known. What God does here, on his reading, is sanction an innocent rite that natural reason had already suggested; its use in false religions is not treated as barring it from the true.

Gill offers a plainer reason alongside. A sanctuary in which beasts were continually slaughtered had a civil need for something to carry off the smell; but the chief reason is religious, to signify that the service done there was acceptable. Calvin sharpens the same point into the altar's whole purpose. The Gentiles burned incense without knowing what it was for, thinking the bare sign discharged them; here God assures his people that the worship they bring at his command goes up to him as a sweet savour, and at the same time warns them to come cleansed, lest any uncleanness profane it. The first altar was for the victims that propitiate; this one perfumes those sacrifices so that they may be accepted — which is why it stands as near the ark as the veil allows, that its savour may rise straight to God. And the type, Calvin adds with David, applies particularly to prayer.

The specifications are read against the altar already described. Keil and Delitzsch give the dimensions and note that the plating ran over the top and down the walls to the ground, which is why it is elsewhere simply called the golden altar. Clarke works the cubits into feet and inches and observes that it was twice as high as it was broad. Ellicott makes the smallness the point: the same shape as the brazen altar but a fraction of its size, a space quite ample for burning so precious a material, which could only be offered in small quantities. He explains the crown as a raised rim to keep what lay on top from falling off, notes that the horns were of one piece with the altar, and accounts for there being two rings here where the larger altar had four: this one was light enough to need no more. The word rendered corners, he adds, means ribs, that is, sides. Clarke identifies the wood as the same used throughout, plentiful and durable, and gives the Septuagint's word for it: incorruptible.

Henry and Wesley both notice something the description omits. There is no grate for ashes to fall into; instead a golden censer was brought with coals in it and set on the altar, the incense burned in the censer, and the coals carried away with it, so that neither coal nor ash ever touched the altar itself. They set beside it the altar of Ezekiel's temple, twice these dimensions, called an altar of wood with no gold mentioned at all — which they take to signify that the incense of gospel times should be spiritual, the worship plain and the service enlarged, since in every place incense is to be offered.
6:
Where exactly the altar stood is settled from several directions. Gill puts it in the holy place and not within the veil, and cites Josephus for its standing between the candlestick and the table, with the Talmudists and Maimonides agreeing that the two flanked it and the altar was in the middle. Ellicott adds that it stood nearer the veil than either of them, which is why the Epistle to the Hebrews can speak of it as belonging in a sense to the holiest — and he distinguishes the veil meant here, the one before the ark, from the curtain at the entrance.

Clarke thinks part of the verse should not be there at all. The clause about the mercy seat looks to him like a copyist's repetition of the clause before it, one Hebrew word having been corrupted into a similar one; and as it stands it would put the altar of incense inside the holy of holies, which cannot be, since this altar was served daily and that place was entered once a year. He reports the five words missing from twenty-six manuscripts and from the Samaritan, and thinks the verse reads better without them. Ellicott, taking the clause as it stands, makes the relation between the two pieces of furniture the point: the altar was the instrument by which the mercy enthroned there was made available to a penitent.

The morning service is described from two sides, the practical and the symbolic. Clarke glosses the dressing of the lamps as preparing the wicks and putting in fresh oil for the evening, and gives the plain reason for the perfume — where so many animals were slaughtered, so much blood sprinkled and so much flesh burnt, something pleasing was needed against the smells, and needed through every part of the tabernacle and its surroundings; he notes in passing that no blood was ever put on this altar except on the one day of general expiation. Ellicott takes the offering of incense to have accompanied both the morning and the evening sacrifice, and reads it as symbolical of prayer.

Gill supplies what the practice had become by later times. A common priest obtained the duty by lot, as in the days of Zacharias; the incense was fetched from the house where it was made, and the coals were gathered from the altar of burnt offering, moved to and fro on its top and carried down in a silver censer to be poured into a golden one, the incense then spread on them and burnt. Wesley gives the double reason for the whole thing: not only to take away the ill smell of the flesh burnt daily on the other altar, but for the honour of God — so that where the offerings on the brazen altar made satisfaction for what had displeased him, this one recommended to his acceptance what his people had done well.
8:
The evening half of the service is described in the same practical detail. Gill has the priest going into the holy place at evening to light the lamps that had gone out, and burning incense on the altar at the same time, so that as the daily sacrifice was offered morning and evening the incense went up with it and much about the same hour. He reports the Jewish account of the exact moment on either side — the morning incense between the sprinkling of the blood and the laying of the pieces on the altar, the evening incense between the pieces and the drink offering — and notes that Philo agrees, having the most fragrant odours offered twice daily at sunrise and sunset, before the morning sacrifice and after the evening one.

The restrictions are absolute and the witnesses read them narrowly. Clarke and Ellicott agree that this was an altar for incense and nothing else, every other offering belonging to the brazen altar, and that strange incense means simply any not compounded as prescribed. Gill turns the prohibition into its spiritual counterpart — to employ other mediators than Christ, or to plead the merit of our own works, is to offer strange incense.

The yearly atonement closes the section, and its object is the altar itself. Gill dates it to the day of atonement on the authority of the Targum of Jonathan, Jarchi and Aben Ezra, and observes that as the altar of burnt offering was first expiated and then used, so this one had an atonement made not merely upon it but for it. Clarke fixes the day as the tenth of the seventh month. Keil and Delitzsch explain that the blood of the sin offering purified it from the uncleannesses of the children of Israel, and that the text says upon it where it might have said upon the horns because the altar was expiated in its horns. Ellicott takes the verse as settling a disputed identification: where some have supposed that the altar before the Lord in Leviticus 16:18 means the brazen one, this passage shows the high priest, having sprinkled the mercy seat, going out to this altar and putting the blood of the bullock and of the goat upon its horns round about. Wesley has him take it in his way as he came out of the holy of holies, and reads the impurity as coming from the sins of the priests who ministered there and of the people for whom they ministered.

Calvin draws the correspondence between the two altars. Sacrifices would not please God unless uncleanness were wiped away by pure prayers, and yet the altar of prayer had itself to be sprinkled with blood — so that the people might learn their prayers obtained acceptance through sacrifice, and had no sweet savour except as sprinkled with the blood of atonement. Done once a year, he adds, it was to be called to mind daily. Wesley turns the pair into a typology: the brazen altar in the court a type of Christ dying on earth, the golden altar in the sanctuary a type of Christ interceding in heaven, who always appears in the presence of God for us. From there he draws the devotional lessons — prayer set forth before God as incense in Psalm 141:2; the smoke ascending as our desires must, kindled with the fire of holy love; a perpetual incense, because we must pray always; the lamps dressed at the very hour it burned, so that reading the scriptures should accompany prayer. What makes such prayers acceptable is the incense Christ adds to them, and his blood atoning for the guilt that cleaves to our best services. His last word is a caution: if the heart and life are not holy, even incense is an abomination.
11:
The formula that opens this section, and opens three more before the chapter ends, is itself read as evidence. Henry and Wesley both take the repetition of the Lord spake unto Moses to mean that these precepts were not delivered in one continuous discourse but with many intermissions, giving Moses time to write down what was said or at least to fix it in his memory; Henry sets beside it Christ giving his disciples instruction as they were able to hear it. Keil and Delitzsch place the atonement money first among the supplementary instructions about the sanctuary, where it completes the earlier demand for freewill offerings.

Ellicott reads the numbering as a formal enrolment and registration. Nothing but a rough estimate had been attempted before; now that a covenant had been made, an exact account of those inside it was wanted, and the wish for such statistics would come naturally to a man trained in Egyptian habits. Gill allows that a census was proper enough in itself, particularly in time of war, but thinks the present one was for the sake of raising money for the tabernacle and its service. Calvin annexes the tribute to the first commandment. Princes number their subjects to take the measure of their own power, but God, who needs no help from men, would have Israel testify by some sign that they lived in subjection to the one who had redeemed them; and because they had been Pharaoh's servants, their freedom would have been unlawful had he not authorised and maintained it. When David numbered the people he was in effect emancipating them from that subjection, which is why the presumption of it was so severely punished. Keil traces the word behind ransom to the idea of covering, the object for which expiation is made being thereby withdrawn from the view of the one to be reconciled.

How often the tax fell is left open. Henry and Wesley report three views: that it belonged only to the first numbering, and was meant to make up what the voluntary contributions had left short; that it recurred whenever the people were numbered, in which case David's offence lay partly in not demanding it; and that it was, as many of the Jewish writers held, an annual tribute merely begun under Moses. Henry adds that men were appointed in every city to receive it yearly, and that this was the tribute money Christ paid rather than give offence, though he showed good reason why he should have been excused. Calvin identifies it with the didrachma of Matthew 17:24 and thinks the right to it was transferred to the Romans at the conquest — the payment that had marked Israel as belonging to God alone being taken from them, on his reading, just before Christ came, so that the new oppression might sharpen their longing for him.

What the ransom was for Ellicott puts in terms of the man paying it. On being formally enrolled among the people of God it would come home to a man how unworthy he was of such a favour and how necessary it was that atonement should somehow be made for him; and God appointed one way for all, to teach that all souls were of equal value in his sight and that unworthiness, whatever its degree, required the same expiation. The threatened plague he reads from the same angle: a man who did not feel his need of a ransom, and gladly pay the small sum at which it was fixed, would show himself proud and presumptuous enough to provoke it.
13:
Gill begins with a practical question the verse settles sideways. Following Jarchi, he says the sum of the people was not taken by counting heads at all: every man gave his half shekel, and the number was known by counting what was paid.

On the coin itself the two calculations differ. Clarke makes the shekel twenty gerahs and the gerah, on Maimonides' reckoning, sixteen barleycorns, the whole shekel three hundred and twenty grains of pure silver; he puts its value at about three shillings, and so the redemption money at eighteenpence. Ellicott arrives at a rather higher figure. Shekels, when they came to be coined, were round pieces of silver about the circumference of a shilling but considerably thicker, averaging some two hundred and twenty grains troy and worth about two shillings and sevenpence; but in Moses' time coins were unknown, and the half shekel would have been a small unstamped lump of perhaps a hundred and ten grains. The ransom was doubtless made this light, he thinks, so that the payment should not be felt practically as a burden by anyone.

Both take the phrase about the shekel of the sanctuary to name a standard rather than a mint. Clarke has the standard by which the value of coin was ascertained kept in the sanctuary itself; Ellicott, that without a standard laid up somewhere weights and measures always fluctuate largely, and that even with one they vary considerably in practice — the sanctuary shekel being a weight kept carefully by the priests along with the vessels, by which all offerings were to be estimated. He would also read the clause about twenty gerahs as defining the shekel, that is, the sanctuary shekel, rather than shekels in general, and glosses gerah as literally a bean, probably of the carob or locust tree, which came to name a weight of about eleven grains troy just as our own grain did.

Clarke draws a series of inferences from the arrangement and does not soften any of them. The life of every man was reckoned forfeit to divine justice, and this was the price at which it was bought back. The redemption money, used in the service of the sanctuary, was ultimately devoted to the profit of those who gave it. The rich were not to give more nor the poor less, which signifies that all souls were equally precious in God's sight and that no difference of outward circumstances could affect the state of a soul, since all had sinned and all must be redeemed by the same price. The atonement had to be made so that there should be no plague, which intimates that a plague or curse must light on the souls for whom no atonement is made. And the whole was to be a memorial, bringing their past deliverance to remembrance and keeping their future redemption in view. Keil and Delitzsch read the memorial the same way: Moses was to appropriate the money to the work of the sanctuary, and by that appropriation it became a permanent reminder of their expiation before the Lord.

Clarke closes where Peter does. This mode of atonement was ineffectual in itself and only pointed out the great sacrifice to be made in the fullness of time for the sin of the world — they were redeemed not with corruptible things, silver and gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish and without spot, foreordained before the foundation of the world.
14:
Who was liable is drawn narrowly. Gill lists Levites, Israelites, proselytes and freed servants as paying, and excludes women, bondservants and children. Ellicott explains the age by Hebrew practice: a man was not reckoned full grown till twenty, and twenty was the point at which liability to military service began and at which the Levites entered on their work in the sanctuary. The two notes sit together instructively: the tribe set apart for the tabernacle is on Gill's list of those who paid, and the year that opened its service to a man is the same year that made him liable for the tax which built what he served in.

The clause forbidding the rich to give more and the poor less draws the fullest comment. Gill takes it to show that the Israelites were alike in God's esteem, their worldly circumstances making no difference — their souls being alike, the same ransom price was given for them, and they were all to have an equal share in the service and the sanctuary. The sum was fixed low enough that the poorest man could pay it, and Gill cites Maimonides for the rule that a man living on alms must beg it of others, or sell the clothes off his back, rather than let it go unpaid. From there he presses the equality further than the verse takes it. Some sins and some sinners are greater than others, and some are redeemed from more sins than others; but all sins are infinite as committed against an infinite God, and so one price is paid for all, the precious blood of Christ, an infinite and divine person — from which it follows that all the ransomed have the same faith, the same righteousness, the same salvation and the same eternal life.

What became of the silver Ellicott answers from the record of the building. The tax brought in above a hundred talents, and the metal was employed for the sockets that supported the boards of the tabernacle and those of the pillars of the veil, together with the hooks for the pillars of the court, their capitals and their connecting rods. So for as long as the tabernacle stood, the precious metal paid as ransom remained in sight of the people, a continual reminder of the position into which their covenant with God had brought them. Gill, glossing the atonement money more simply, calls the half shekel the ransom of their souls.
17:
Keil and Delitzsch account for how little is said here. The laver is added in a supplementary way and never described, because of the subordinate position it held: it was not directly connected with the sanctuary but served only to cleanse the priests for the performance of their duties. The word for it means a round, caldron-shaped basin, which Clarke notes can stand for a caldron elsewhere; he takes it for any large round vessel used to wash hands and feet. Ellicott would render the metal bronze rather than brass, and pictures a large urn or vase carried on a comparatively slender stem rising from a pedestal, of the kind shown in the Assyrian bas-reliefs.

What the text calls its foot is the one point on which the readings pull apart. Clarke takes it to mean simply the pedestal the laver stood on. Keil and Delitzsch argue the opposite, that it was not the base at all but something separate from the basin, used for drawing off as much water as was wanted — their evidence being that it is always mentioned alongside the laver rather than assumed in it, which they read as a mark of independence. Henry and Wesley suppose a third arrangement, a foot so contrived as to receive the water let down into it out of the laver by spouts or cocks.

Its position was fixed by what it was for. Ellicott points out that it had to stand near the altar, since the priests washed at it on every occasion of ministering there, and near the entrance, since they washed again before going into the holy place; Jewish tradition, he adds, put it between the two, though not exactly between them but a little to the south. He also lists the other uses the water served: the washing of certain parts of the victim, and probably the cleansing of the altar and the ground about it from bloodstains.

Calvin explains why he treats the laver here rather than with the other vessels: bare mention of a water-pot would have profited the reader nothing, and it is the command that water be always ready in it that shows the reverence and sanctity God required in his service. He sets the Gentile parallel beside it without granting it anything. It was a common proverb among them that men were guilty of impiety who handled holy things with unwashen hands, and their poets could bid the profane keep away from the sacrifices, or make a man refuse to touch the household gods till he had cleansed himself in some living stream — expressions that seem almost to hit the right point but were a fleeting imagination only, since no desire to propitiate God had been awakened in them, and their minds, darkened with error, did not know what the rite meant. His own reading is that the washing of hands and feet denoted that every part of the body was infected, since Scripture uses hands for the actions of life and likens a whole life to a journey.

Henry and Wesley describe the practice: clean water was put in fresh every day, and however clean a man had washed at home it would not serve, because the laver was what washing had been appointed for. They read it as designed to teach purity in every ministration and a dread of the pollutions of sin: the priests were not only washed clean when first consecrated but kept clean every time they went in, since he only shall stand in God's holy place that has clean hands and a pure heart. Gill and Henry take the vessel forward instead of sideways: this was a laver for the priests only, where what is opened now is a fountain for Judah and Jerusalem, and an inexhaustible one, so that if we remain in our pollution the fault is our own.
19:
The washing was done at the laver, not in it. Gill is careful about the preposition and fills it out from the rabbis: the vessel had spouts or mouths from which the water flowed, and Bartenora is cited for the priests washing from water running out of it rather than out of the basin itself. Two spouts were there at first; Ben Katin made twelve, so that twelve priests could wash at one time, and Jarchi and Ben Melech describe them doing hands and feet together, the right hand laid on the right foot and the left on the left. Gill adds that the laver stood near the door, so that they washed as soon as they entered, and that no man went into the court before washing — not though he were clean, not though he had contracted no filthiness, not though he had already washed his hands and feet at home.

Why those two parts of the body is answered the same way by several hands. Ellicott takes washing the hands for purity in act and washing the feet for holiness in all the walk and conversation. Gill reads the hands as the instruments of action and the feet of walking, and concludes that the works of good men and their whole conversation are not without sin, and so need daily washing in the blood of Christ. Gill draws the practical consequence for the worshipper as well as the priest: pure hands are as necessary as a pure heart for compassing the altar of God and for prayer, in which holy hands are to be lifted up.

The threatened death makes Ellicott pause. He finds it not altogether easy to see why the penalty was attached to the neglect of some ceremonial observances and not others, and settles the question by the ease of the thing: ablution was so simple, and probably so long established, that to omit it would imply intentional disrespect toward God. Gill reasons identically from the other end — the easier the command, the more inexcusable the neglect and the greater the severity it deserved. Clarke reads the washing as emblematic of the whole conduct, the hands standing for all their works and the feet for all their goings, both of which had to be holiness to the Lord; he notes that it was needful in a plain way, since the priests ministered barefoot, but equally needful for the guilt they might have contracted, and calls it what Paul calls the laver of regeneration, whose renewing must be repeated as often as any defilement is.

On the statute lasting for ever the two readings agree in substance. Ellicott divides it: the external act was to continue as long as the dispensation did, while the internal purity it symbolised would be required of everyone entering the divine presence for ever. Clarke divides it the same way and then presses it on gospel ministers — each time they minister in public, in the word or the sacraments, they should see to it that they have a fresh application of the grace and Spirit of Christ, to do away past unfaithfulness and to make their ministrations spirit and life to the people. Gill ends on the severity rather than the comfort: the death threatened would come by the immediate hand of God, who would so greatly resent a neglect of this command, and the repetition of the warning is there so that they might observe it carefully and not perish.
22:
Gill places the fresh word a little later, while Moses was still on the mount. Henry states the principle before touching the recipe: with these preparations God was to be honoured, and therefore he would appoint the making of them, since nothing comes to God but what comes from him. On the ingredients he declines to be certain — interpreters are not agreed — while holding that they were the best and fittest for the purpose, as they must be when divine wisdom appointed them for the divine honour.

The method he does describe. It was to be compounded after the art of the apothecary: the spices, amounting in all to nearly half a hundredweight, were infused in the oil, itself about five or six quarts, and then strained out again, leaving an admirable sweet smell behind in the oil. With that oil the tent and all its furniture were to be anointed, and it served besides in the consecration of the priests, and was to be continued throughout their generations. The incense compounded later in the chapter he pairs with it as a second preparation of sweet spices, though of spices not so rare and rich as these.

Both preparations were meant to be prized. Henry finds in them a demonstration of the excellency of holiness — that there stood in the tabernacle something in the highest degree grateful to the sight and to the smell — and moves from the oil to what Scripture makes of it, Christ's name being as ointment poured forth and the good name of a Christian better than precious ointment.

The same law covers both, and Henry reads it as guarding reverence. That the like should not be made for any common use was God's way of preserving in the people's minds a regard for his own institutions, and it teaches us not to profane or abuse anything by which God makes himself known — the fault of those who invented for their common entertainments instruments of music like David's. To jest with sacred things is a great affront to him, and to make sport with his word and ordinances or treat them with lightness is the same offence in another form. What is God's peculiar must not be handled as a common thing; and Henry ends on the sharpest case of the abuse, which is to use a profession of the gospel of Christ to forward some worldly interest of one's own.
23:
Clarke sets out the proportions and converts them. Five hundred shekels each of myrrh and cassia come to something over forty-eight pounds apiece, the two hundred and fifty each of cinnamon and calamus to a little over twenty-four, and the hin of olive oil to about five quarts. Myrrh he calls the produce of an oriental tree not well known, gathered by making an incision in it, and holds that what now goes by the name is precisely what the ancients meant; olive oil he takes to be the best preservative of odours there is. Since the gifts and graces of the Spirit are themselves called an anointing, he reads the whole compound as an emblem of them.

Ellicott works through the four spices and disagrees with him on the first. Principal spices is not loose praise — the East produced a great variety, but a few were always favoured, and Herodotus names five that Arabia furnished to other countries, at least two of them seemingly these. The Hebrew behind pure myrrh he renders myrrh of freedom, the purest and best sort, which exudes from the shrub of itself; the inferior kind is what is got by cutting the bark, which is the method Clarke describes. Its ancient uses he traces widely: a main element in the best Egyptian embalming, prized in Persia as an odour, used by the Greeks in unguents, applied by later Jews as an antiseptic to corpses. This is its first mention in Scripture, the word so translated in Genesis being properly ladanum.

Cinnamon he makes the opposite case, one of the rarest where myrrh was among the commonest — the produce of a tree allied to the laurel which now grows only in Ceylon, Sumatra, China and on the Malabar coast. Herodotus and Strabo report it growing anciently in Arabia, which he doubts, thinking the Arabians imported it and passed it to the Phoenicians. Sweet calamus he leaves open: several distinct aromatic reeds grew in the East, one of them in Syria near Lebanon on Pliny's report, and which species is meant here he will not say.

Calvin takes the expense itself as instruction — a composition exquisite in costliness and odour, set before a people still rude so that their senses might be affected and they lifted by steps toward spiritual things. What it typifies he thinks past controversy: the Holy Spirit, since the metaphor of anointing runs everywhere through the prophets when they speak of the Spirit's gifts, and God in anointing kings testified that he would endow them with prudence and justice. The tabernacle was sprinkled that Israel might learn how little every exercise of piety profits without the Spirit's secret operation, and Aaron anointed because Christ was consecrated by the Spirit to be Mediator between God and man. Keil and Delitzsch account for the compound's holiness either way — either because it was made of the four fragrant substances in the proportions commanded, or because God declared this kind of mixture holy — and note that he forbade for all time, on pain of death, both the use of ointment so prepared for ordinary anointings and any imitation of it.

Wesley follows the oil's later history and finds a providence in its end. Solomon was anointed with it and some other of the kings, and the high priests with enough of it to run down to the skirts of their garments; the making of it up is on record afterwards. All agree there was none of this holy oil in the second temple, which he puts down to a notion that it was no longer lawful to make it — a want overruled, on his reading, to be a presage of the better unction of the Holy Ghost in gospel times, the variety of whose gifts these several sweet ingredients had typified.
24:
Ellicott finishes the list with cassia and is exact about the word. The Hebrew here is not the term used elsewhere, though the best Hebrew authorities take both to mean cassia, deriving them from roots that signify splitting or peeling off. What is meant is the inner bark of a tree native to India, Java and the Malay peninsula, nearly the same in flavour as cinnamon but more pungent and of a coarser texture; the word itself occurs in Scripture only here and once in Ezekiel 27:19.

The compounding was not to be rough work. Clarke glosses the apothecary as a compounder or confectioner, anyone who puts drugs and aromatics together. Ellicott presses the point: skill was to be called in, the spices not pounded and mixed with the oil in some rude and unscientific way but composed by the best art of the time — and he reports the Jewish tradition that the essence was first drawn off from each spice separately and the oil then mingled with the essences. Gill adds what the result was like, not thick as ointments usually are but a liquid that could be poured, which is why it is called an oil of ointment; and holy, because devoted to sacred uses only.

Calvin reads the word holy the other way round, from its effect rather than its ingredients — nothing is accounted pure without it, just as the Spirit of God sanctifies ourselves and everything of ours, since apart from him we are unholy and all that belongs to us corrupt. The command that the ceremony run through all the generations of that people he takes to carry an implied contrast with the church that came after, which wants no shadows now that the substance has appeared; the only begotten Son rightly bears the name Christ because by coming he abolished these figures, and Simeon, taking him in his arms and calling him the Lord's Christ, taught that the external use of the legal oil had ceased.

From that he turns on a later practice, and the judgment is his alone among these voices. To anoint priests and altars in imitation of the Jews he calls a superstition, as though those who did it desired to bury Christ again with their ointments, and he asks that the invention be held in detestation as blasphemous for overthrowing the limits God prescribed. The prohibition on making the like of it he explains more mildly: ointments belonged then among the luxuries of a fine banquet, and to put this one to that use was profanation, the reason given in the text being simply that what is holy may be holy to them. Sacred things divinely instituted always keep their nature, he grants, and cannot be corrupted or made void by our vices — but by our filthiness, our impure use of them or our neglect, we pollute them so far as in us lies.
26:
Ellicott sets out the order in which the oil was to travel. The tabernacle and its contents were consecrated first and the priests after; within the tent the anointing began with the ark in the holiest, went on to the holy place for the table and its vessels, the candlestick and the altar of incense, and only then passed the veil into the outer court, where the oil was sprinkled on the brazen altar and on the laver. Gill adds a qualification about how much of the fabric was touched: it cannot be thought the whole was anointed all over, but a part of it for the whole. The brazen altar, he notes, was sprinkled seven times.

What the anointing signified he reads at every stop. The tent itself he takes for the human nature of Christ, the true tabernacle God pitched and not man, which was anointed with the Holy Ghost — or else for the church, itself a holy temple that receives the unction from the Holy One. The table with its rings and staves and dishes he refers to the communion of Christ's people with him, feeding on the food that endures. And where the text says the vessels were sanctified to be most holy, he presses the comparison: if oil could make furniture most holy, how much more must the grace of the Spirit do so for those who partake of it — a holiness at present imperfect, but one that will be completed, since without it no man shall see the Lord.

On the anointing of the priests three readings converge. Gill has it confined to Aaron and his sons and no others, following Aben Ezra, and takes them for a type of Christ anointed with the Spirit without measure to his offices of prophet, priest and king, and of all the saints who are made priests to God. Clarke reads the oil as an emblem of divine teaching, and particularly of those influences by which the church was at the beginning guided into all truth — the unction received from the Holy One which abides, so that they need not that any man teach them. Ellicott turns it into a requirement: as Aaron and his sons were unfit to minister until the holy oil had been poured on them, so Christian ministers can be fitted for their office no otherwise than by receiving that effluence of the Spirit which the oil typified.

The prohibition is read strictly and then made precise. Gill glosses the clause about man's flesh as meaning common men, on whom oil was poured freely enough at eastern feasts and entertainments — though it was poured on flesh in one case, running down from Aaron's head to his beard. Ellicott draws the line where the recipe does: the ingredients might be used in unguents separately, and even united in proportions other than these, but combined in the proportions fixed for the holy oil they were to have no secular employment whatever. Gill marks the reach of the penalty at the same place: it falls on whoever compounds the like of it for his own use, or for any purpose other than the one God appointed it for.
34:
The four ingredients are identified twice over, and not always to the same result. Clarke takes stacte for what was afterwards called the balm of Jericho, the gum that flows of itself from the tree that yields myrrh; onycha for the outer crust of a shell-fish, the basis, he says, of the principal perfumes of the East Indies; galbanum for an African ferula that yields a thin cream-coloured milk wherever it is broken; frankincense for a dry resin in pale yellowish drops, strong-smelling and bitter to the taste, from a tree not well known, reported by Dioscorides to be got in India. Ellicott would drop the epithet altogether — the Hebrew says only spices — and observes that incense elsewhere in the ancient world was usually a single spice, most often frankincense, where the Hebrew article was always compounded; Josephus reports thirteen ingredients in the incense of the later temple. He differs from Clarke at three of the four: gum storax from a tree common in Syria and Palestine, which burns readily and gives off much smoke; the claw of a shell-fish of the Red Sea; and a galbanum procurable from several plants. Frankincense he thinks the main element here, drawn from incisions in the bark of a tree growing abundantly in India, and anciently in Arabia, whence Egyptians, Phoenicians and Greeks all drew it in quantity.

Over galbanum the two part company outright. Ellicott reports its odour when burnt as pungent and disagreeable in itself, but valued because it brings out and prolongs the scent of the other spices. Calvin will not have it. He declines to discuss the ingredients — let the curious do that if they please — holding it enough that they were chosen at God's will to make a very sweet smell; and against those who suppose galbanum ill-savoured he answers that a conjecture in an unknown matter deserves little credit. His own conviction is that it was sweet, and he argues it from the text: the death penalty on making such a perfume for private gratification would be absurd unless the odour were very agreeable, and the analogy between the sign and the thing signified would not hold unless that sweetness testified how greatly God is pleased with the prayers of his people.

Wesley reports the Jewish account of the quantity, a pound for each day of the year and three pounds over for the day of atonement, and finds a figure in the beating small: thus it pleased the Lord to bruise the Redeemer when he offered himself a sacrifice of a sweet-smelling savour. Keil and Delitzsch read the word rendered tempered together as salted, seasoned with salt like the meat offering, and argue that it cannot mean mixed or rubbed to powder, since the pulverising is expressed by a different word in the verse after. Ellicott gives both sides — the older versions have tempered together, most moderns have salted, and the word will carry either — and notes that Bezaleel's art was called in for the incense as for the oil.

Clarke reads the penalty as excommunication, the offender losing all right and interest in the promises of God, and takes the prohibition as a specimen of how carefully God guards his worship from being adulterated by human invention. Arts and sciences may fairly be called men's inventions; religion is both the gift and the invention of God, and the worship he has prescribed is what will please him. Nadab and Abihu offering strange fire, and their destruction, he sets down as a lasting warning to anyone who would model God's religion by his own caprice. Calvin gives the plainer reason for the ban: since men are rude and earthly-minded, nothing is more likely than that they should mix heavenly things with earthly, and so what was peculiarly holy had to be kept clear of common use.
36:
Gill takes the beating small to cover the whole of the compound and not some portion of it, and gives practical reasons rather than symbolic ones: reduced fine, the spices mixed together the better, spread more easily over the coals, and sent their smoke up the sooner. Nothing in the wording, on his reading, marks off one part of the incense for a different usage from the rest.

Where the incense was to lie is settled against the reading the words first suggest. Keil and Delitzsch insist that before the testimony does not mean inside the most holy place but the spot where the altar of incense stood, and they refer back to the earlier placing of that altar in this chapter, and across to the day of atonement, for the same way of speaking; the remainder of the stock, they add, was of course kept elsewhere. Ellicott arrives at the same position from the other side, and is interested less in excluding the wrong room than in what the arrangement taught: some pieces of the incense were to be continually before the ark of the covenant, either on the golden altar or perhaps at its base ready for offering, and a supply always lying there symbolised the need for the perpetual offering of prayer. The two are guarding different things — one against lodging the incense in a room the priests entered once a year, the other in favour of a store kept always within reach of the altar where it was burnt.

The closing ban repeats the one laid on the anointing oil, and Keil and Delitzsch treat the two as a single provision, forbidding both the imitation of the composition and the turning of it to any strange use; the phrase about smelling to it they gloss simply as enjoying its perfume. Gill draws the line more finely than the verse does, following Jarchi. A man might make up the very same ingredients in the very same weights, exactly like it, and be guiltless — if he made it and sold it to the congregation. What brought the sentence down was making it for his own delight and pleasure; that, and not the compounding as such, is what the cutting off from his people answers to.
